body:
Installed capacity and electricity generation

Installed capacity is the rated power output of an installed electricity-generating facility. It is commonly expressed in megawatts (MW) or gigawatts (GW). In contrast, electricity generation is the amount of electrical energy actually produced over a period. It is measured in units such as kilowatt-hours (kWh), gigawatt-hours (GWh) or billion units (BU).

The basic unit relationships are:

  • 1 GW = 1,000 MW.
  • 1 GWh = 1 million kWh.
  • 1 BU = 1 billion kWh.

Installed capacity does not tell us how much electricity a plant actually produced. A solar plant may have a high rated capacity but produce no electricity at night. Wind output varies with wind conditions. Actual generation also depends on plant availability, maintenance and grid conditions.

Gujarat's installed renewable capacity

According to the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy's state-wise installed-capacity statement as on 30 September 2026, Gujarat had the following capacities. These are installed figures for that date, not future targets.

CategoryCapacity (MW)Meaning
Ground-mounted solar25,902.07Solar plants installed on land
Rooftop solar8,525.10Solar installations on rooftops
Solar component of hybrids1,606.86Solar capacity reported under hybrid projects
Off-grid solar and relevant KUSUM component200.53Other solar capacity in the stated category
Total solar36,234.55All reported solar categories
Wind17,043.76Installed wind capacity
Total renewable capacity55,511.46Solar, wind, bioenergy and hydro categories

Thus, Gujarat's reported solar capacity was about 36.23 GW, wind capacity about 17.04 GW, and total renewable capacity about 55.51 GW on 30 September 2026. The total renewable figure includes technologies other than solar and wind, including large hydropower.

What the generation figures show

MNRE's RE-Statistics 2025-26 reports that Gujarat generated approximately 67.83 BU of renewable electricity during the financial year 2025-26. Wind contributed approximately 33.71 BU and solar approximately 27.38 BU.

These figures show that wind supplied more renewable electricity than solar during that financial year, even though the later September 2026 capacity snapshot shows more installed solar capacity than wind capacity. The two observations describe different measurements and different reporting periods; they are not contradictory.

Capacity is measured in MW or GW; generation is measured in kWh, GWh or BU. Storage capacity is often described in MWh or GWh, while its charging or discharging power is measured in MW or GW.

Why transmission matters

Large renewable plants often operate far from major consumers. Electricity from a solar park or wind farm is collected, connected to suitable substations and transmitted through the grid towards demand centres. In Gujarat, the Gujarat Energy Transmission Corporation Limited (GETCO) is an important state transmission utility. Distribution companies supply electricity through distribution networks to consumers.

Transmission and distribution have different roles. Transmission moves large quantities of power between major network points, while distribution delivers power to end users. Insufficient evacuation or transmission capacity may prevent some available renewable electricity from reaching consumers.

Electricity supply and demand must remain balanced. When renewable output changes rapidly, grid operators may use other generating sources, storage, demand management or appropriate operating arrangements to maintain reliable supply. Deliberately reducing available renewable generation when necessary is called curtailment.

Storage and flexibility

MethodBasic principleMain application
Battery energy storage systemStores electrical energy in batteries and releases it laterShifting solar output to later hours and supporting grid flexibility
Pumped-storage hydropowerUses electricity to pump water uphill and releases it through turbines laterStoring and returning electricity where suitable reservoirs and elevations exist
Green hydrogenUses renewable energy to produce a fuel that can be stored and used laterIndustrial fuel and feedstock, and some longer-duration energy applications

A battery stores energy; it does not create a new primary energy resource. Pumped storage similarly returns energy that was previously used to move water uphill, with some losses. Hydrogen is an energy carrier: energy is used to produce it, and it can later provide energy or act as an industrial raw material. Converting electricity to hydrogen and then back to electricity generally involves greater energy losses than directly storing electricity in batteries.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat's reported solar capacity on 30 September 2026 was 36,234.55 MW.
  • Its reported wind capacity on the same date was 17,043.76 MW.
  • Gujarat generated 67.83 BU of renewable electricity during 2025-26.
  • During 2025-26, wind generation exceeded solar generation in Gujarat.
  • GETCO is associated with electricity transmission in Gujarat.
  • Trap: MW measures power, while MWh measures energy; planned capacity is not installed capacity.

[Sources: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, State-wise Location-based Installed Capacity of Renewable Power as on 30 September 2026, Gujarat row; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, RE-Statistics 2025-26, Chapter 11, Gujarat, Section 11.3, Energy Generation during 2025-26, printed p. 60; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, printed p. 30; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Policy and Regulatory Updates, December 2025, Gujarat Integrated Renewable Energy Policy 2025 summary, grid strengthening and BESS provisions; official statistical and policy sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Hydrogen as an energy carrier and industrial material

Hydrogen is an element that can be used as a fuel or an industrial raw material. It is not a naturally available primary energy source in the same sense as sunlight or wind. Commercial hydrogen usually has to be produced using energy and other inputs.

Hydrogen can release energy when used in a suitable fuel cell or combustion system. A fuel cell combines hydrogen with oxygen to produce electricity, with water as the principal direct reaction product. However, the environmental impact of using hydrogen depends strongly on how the hydrogen was produced.

How electrolysis produces hydrogen

Electrolysis uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. An electrolyser is the equipment that carries out this process.

Its overall chemical reaction is:

2H2O → 2H2 + O2

When the electricity comes from eligible renewable sources and the production meets the applicable emissions standard, the resulting hydrogen can qualify as green hydrogen.

Solar and wind plants can supply renewable electricity for electrolysis. Because renewable output varies, a hydrogen project may use a combination of renewable sources, storage, grid arrangements and controlled production schedules.

Green, grey and blue hydrogen

Hydrogen typeTypical production routeKey distinction
Green hydrogenRenewable-energy-based production, commonly water electrolysisMust satisfy the applicable renewable-energy and emissions requirements
Grey hydrogenUsually produced from fossil fuels such as natural gas without capturing the associated carbon dioxideProduction normally causes substantial greenhouse gas emissions
Blue hydrogenFossil-fuel-based production with carbon capture and storage or carbon capture, utilisation and storageCaptures some associated emissions but is not automatically emission-free

These terms describe the production route and associated emissions, not the visible colour of hydrogen gas. Hydrogen is colourless.

India's Green Hydrogen Standard, issued by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy on 18 August 2023, defines green hydrogen in terms of renewable energy and specified emissions limits. The definition includes eligible renewable-energy-based production through electrolysis and biomass conversion.

For electrolysis-based green hydrogen, the standard specifies that the covered non-biogenic greenhouse gas emissions from water treatment, electrolysis, purification, drying and compression must not exceed 2 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent per kg of hydrogen, averaged over the previous 12 months. Green hydrogen therefore means production satisfying a defined low-emission standard; it does not mean that every related activity has literally zero emissions.

Water needed for green hydrogen

Electrolysis requires purified water. From the chemical reaction, approximately 9 kg of water, or about 9 litres, is theoretically required to produce 1 kg of hydrogen. Actual industrial water requirements can be higher because water treatment, cooling and other operations also use water.

This distinction is especially important in dry areas of Kachchh and Saurashtra. A coastal plant may obtain water through desalination, followed by the necessary purification, but desalination needs energy and creates a concentrated saline waste stream that must be managed appropriately. Ordinary untreated seawater is not simply a direct substitute for purified water in conventional commercial electrolysers.

Why refineries need hydrogen

Petroleum refineries already consume hydrogen. One important use is removing sulphur compounds from petroleum products through hydrodesulphurisation. Hydrogen is also used in certain processes that convert heavier petroleum fractions into more useful products.

Replacing conventional fossil-based hydrogen with qualifying green hydrogen can reduce emissions associated with hydrogen production. It does not, by itself, make petrol or diesel renewable fuels. Those petroleum products still release carbon dioxide when burned.

Why fertilizer plants need hydrogen

Hydrogen is an important input in the production of ammonia. Ammonia contains nitrogen and hydrogen, with the chemical formula NH3. Nitrogen can be obtained from air, while hydrogen is supplied from an appropriate production process.

Ammonia is a major industrial input for nitrogen fertilizers, including urea. When the hydrogen is produced through a qualifying green route, ammonia made using that hydrogen and appropriate processes may be described as green ammonia. This offers an opportunity to reduce emissions in fertilizer production.

Green ammonia as a transportable product

Hydrogen gas is difficult to store and transport economically over long distances because of its low volumetric energy density under ordinary conditions. It often needs compression, liquefaction or chemical conversion.

Green ammonia is one potential hydrogen-derived product for transport, storage and export. It can serve as a fertilizer input and may also have applications as an energy carrier or fuel. However, ammonia is toxic, requires careful handling and must not be considered harmless simply because its hydrogen was made using renewable electricity.

Prelims focus

  • Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.
  • Hydrogen is an energy carrier and an industrial raw material.
  • India issued its Green Hydrogen Standard on 18 August 2023.
  • The specified emissions threshold is 2 kg CO2 equivalent per kg hydrogen over a 12-month average.
  • Approximately 9 litres of water per kg hydrogen is the theoretical chemical requirement; total industrial use may be higher.
  • Ammonia has the formula NH3 and is a major input for nitrogen fertilizers.
  • Trap: Green hydrogen is not defined merely by the presence of an electrolyser; its energy source and emissions also matter.

[Sources: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Office Memorandum No. 353/35/2022-NT, Green Hydrogen Standard for India, 18 August 2023, paragraphs 1-3; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India, Sections 8-10; Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen production and applications, press note issued November 2026; Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board, Pathways for Transmission of Hydrogen in India, 2025, Water Availability section; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia: Production, Meaning and Industrial Uses
